entries.s: Bedridden individuals should be turned over at least every 2 hours, lying on their side at a 30-degree angle, with pressure applied to bony prominences.
entries.why: Prolonged pressure on the same area can cause pressure injury warning signs within 2 hours; turning over is the cheapest and most effective way to prevent pressure injuries.
steps: First, tell the client what they need to do, and confirm that the bed rails are raised and the bed height is suitable for their waist.
Use a sheet or turning towel to move the body in one piece, avoiding dragging the skin.
Lie on your side at a 30-degree angle (not 90 degrees), with a long pillow for back support, and soft pillows between your knees and ankles.
Raise the head of the bed no more than 30 degrees to avoid shearing forces caused by the body sliding down (except when eating).
After turning over, check the sacrum, hip bone, heels, shoulder blades, and ears: are they red? Do they not turn white when pressed?
Record the time of turning over and the condition of the skin.
no: Do not pull the arms or ankles directly to turn the body.
Do not allow the nasogastric tube or urinary catheter to be pressed under the body.
Do not use a donut-shaped seat cushion, as it will increase blood flow to the central area.
If the redness does not fade when pressed, do not massage the area.
entries.rep: Skin develops non-fading erythema, blisters, or broken skin → Report to supervisor on the same day and request the unit to refer to home care assessment.
entries.ref: Ministry of Health and Welfare's principles for pressure injury prevention; Long-term care payment and reimbursement standards BA10: Turning over and patting the back.
entries.ask: My client, whom I care for, complains of hip pain even after lying on their side at a 30-degree angle. How else can I adjust the pillow position?

entries.s: First, lock the brakes, raise the foot pedals, and attach the relocation belt. Use a "stand-turn-sit" motion instead of carrying.
entries.why: Relocation is the most common time for home care workers to suffer back injuries and for clients to fall. Nine out of ten accidents are caused by not locking the brakes, not retracting the foot pedals, or using force on the back when lifting.
steps: Position the wheelchair to the client's favorable side, at a 30-45 degree angle to the bed. Lock the brakes, raise or remove the footrests, and move the armrests.
Have the client sit on the edge of the bed with both feet flat on the ground and buttocks against the edge. Observe for 30 seconds to see if they feel dizzy.
Help the client fasten the transfer belt, holding the belt but not their clothes; place one foot in front of the other, with knees slightly bent.
Use the command "One, two, three, stand up," instructing the client to push against the bed surface, lean forward, stand up, and turn around using their feet as a pivot.
Ensure the back of the knees touches the wheelchair seat before slowly sitting down, straighten the buttocks, and place the footrests back.
no: Do not pull upwards by grabbing under the armpits (this can strain the shoulder joint).
Do not move the client if they are dizzy or their blood pressure is unstable.
Do not move clients who are completely unable to support their weight or whose weight exceeds their own weight by one person. Use a transfer board or have two people assist.
entries.rep: If the client experiences pain, falls, or you strain your back during the transfer process → report and record according to the abnormal event procedure.
entries.ref: Ministry of Health and Welfare Caregiver Training Materials: Transfer Techniques; Occupational Safety and Health Act: Employers should provide safe operating procedures.
entries.ask: If the client is hemiplegic and can only exert force on one side, which side should the wheelchair be placed on when transferring from bed to wheelchair, and how should the steps be changed?

entries.s: Water temperature 38–40℃. Rinse your wrists first, then rinse the client's. After washing, dry any creases and "observe the skin."
entries.why: Bathing is the only opportunity to fully see the skin of the entire body, and it is also a high-risk period for burns and falls.
steps: Close the windows, turn on the heater or hot air, lay a non-slip mat in the bathroom, and prepare towels and changes of clothes before starting.
Water temperature 38–40℃, test the temperature with the inside of your wrist; use a thermometer for clients with diabetes or impaired sensation.
Sequence: face → upper limbs → torso → lower limbs → back → perineum → buttocks, from clean areas to dirty areas.
While washing, observe: erythema on bony prominences, ulcers between toes, eczema in the armpits and groin, and unexplained bruises.
Dry and keep warm within 3 minutes of washing, ensuring folds (under the breasts, groin, between the toes) are completely dry.
Apply a thin layer of lotion to dry areas; do not apply between the toes.
no: Do not allow the client to stand while showering alone; standing showers should be done with handrails or a shower chair.
Do not soak feet in excessively hot water to "promote circulation," as this can cause burns to diabetic foot ulcers without the client realizing it.
If unexplained bruises or fingerprint-like marks are found, do not pursue blame; record the information first.
entries.rep: New wounds, blisters, unexplained bruises, or ulcers between the toes → report to the supervisor on the same day; if mistreatment is suspected, handle according to the reporting responsibility.
entries.ref: Caregiver training course: body hygiene; long-term care payment and payment standard BA07: assisting with bathing and washing hair.
entries.ask: The client refuses to bathe and gets angry at the mere mention of bathing. What non-coercive methods can be used to guide them?

entries.t: Oral hygiene, including people who are fasting or tube-fed
entries.s: At least twice a day, morning and evening, clean the gums, tongue, and oral mucosa; remove dentures and soak them in water before bed.
entries.why: Ingestion or inhalation of oral bacteria is one of the main causes of aspiration pneumonia in the elderly. Oral hygiene is a way to prevent pneumonia.
steps: The client should sit up or elevate the head of the bed by more than 30 degrees, turn their head to one side, and wrap a towel around their neck.
Use a soft-bristled toothbrush with a small amount of water or fluoride toothpaste to brush the teeth, gums, and tongue; wipe the mucosa with a sponge or gauze.
Patients using nasogastric tubes or those on fasting should be cleaned as before. Use a cotton swab dipped in a small amount of water, wringing it out each time to avoid choking.
Dentures: Brush with a denture brush and water (or denture cleaning tablets). Remove before bedtime and soak in clean water; do not soak in hot water.
Observe during cleaning for: bad breath, leukoplakia, ulcers, bleeding gums, loose or worn dentures.
no: Do not brush vigorously on patients with receding gums or those prone to bleeding; use a sponge instead.
Do not allow the patient to lie flat while cleaning their mouth.
Do not use mouthwash instead of brushing teeth.
entries.rep: If oral ulcers do not heal for more than 2 weeks, leukoplakia, or worn dentures → report to the supervisor and recommend that the family arrange for dental care.
entries.ref: Caregiver training course: Oral care; Ministry of Health and Welfare Oral Health Guidelines.
entries.ask: The client is clenching their teeth and won't let me brush my teeth. What are some safe ways to open their mouth or alternative cleaning methods?

entries.s: Stage I is an erythema that doesn't turn white when pressed; once there is broken skin or blisters, it's Stage II or higher, and must be reported immediately.
entries.why: Home care workers are the people who see the skin most often. Understanding the stages is crucial to knowing when the condition can be reversed by turning the patient over and when nursing intervention is necessary.
steps: Stage I: Intact skin, but with an erythema that doesn't fade when pressed (in darker skin tones, the redness may not be visible; it may be purple or feel hard and hot to the touch) → Increase pressure relief, turn the patient over, and report on the same day.
Stage II: Epidermal damage, superficial ulcers, or blisters → Do not break the blisters, report and request a nursing assessment.
Stage III: Full-thickness skin loss, subcutaneous fat visible → Report, nursing care.
Stage IV: Deep to muscle, tendon, or bone → Report, medical treatment required.
Unstageable/Deep tissue injury: Covered by black scab or purplish-black → Report.
Scan the sacrum, hip, heel, and ischium with your eyes every time you clean, turn the baby, or change diapers.
no: Do not use home remedies, ointments, or disinfectants on the wound yourself.
Do not massage reddened areas.
Do not continue to use the wounded area as a pressure point.
entries.rep: Any stage I or higher pressure injury → Report and supervise home care on the same day; Stage IV or with odor or fever → Report immediately.
entries.ref: NPIAP pressure injury staging; Ministry of Health and Welfare pressure injury prevention and care guidelines.
entries.ask: The client has a patch of purplish-black skin on their sacrum, but it's not broken. What stage is this? What can I do while waiting for the nursing care to arrive?

entries.t: Assistance with eating and safe swallowing
entries.s: Sit upright at a 90-degree angle, chin slightly tucked, take one small bite at a time, make sure the patient has swallowed completely before taking the next bite. Sit for 30 minutes after meals.
entries.why: Choking and aspiration pneumonia are among the main causes of hospitalization for the elderly, and most choking is due to posture and speed.
steps: Before feeding, confirm the client is awake and responsive; for those in bed, elevate the head of the bed at least 60 degrees, and place a pillow behind the head to slightly tuck the chin.
Sit at or slightly below the client's eye level; do not stand and feed from above.
Give one small sip (about one teaspoon) at a time, observing the Adam's apple move up and down and the mouth clear before giving the next sip.
Serve solids and liquids separately; for clients who easily choke on water, use a thickener as directed by a professional.
If coughing, a wet voice, tearing, or rapid breathing occurs during eating, pause and allow the client to cough it all up.
After meals, keep the client seated for at least 30 minutes before assisting with oral hygiene.
no: Do not feed the client when they are sleepy or lying down.
Do not use a straw to give water to clients who easily choke (a straw will cause water to enter the throat too quickly).
Do not speed up the process or use a larger spoon to save time.
Do not feed clients with dentures that are not worn to foods that require chewing.
entries.rep: Recurrent choking, postprandial fever, significantly prolonged eating time, weight loss → Report to supervisor, recommend referral for speech therapy swallowing assessment.
entries.ref: Long-term care reimbursement and payment criteria: BA04 Assisted feeding or tube feeding; BA05 Meal care; Speech therapy swallowing safety principles.
entries.ask: The client chokes every time he drinks water, but not when eating porridge. How can I adjust the texture and posture of the water?

entries.s: For elderly people without a doctor's order to restrict water intake, the daily target is approximately 1500 cc; for constipation, start with water, fiber, activity, and toilet time.
entries.why: Elderly people experience decreased thirst. Dehydration can cause confusion, falls, and urinary tract infections; constipation can cause bloating, loss of appetite, and delirium.
steps: Divide the 1500 cc into visible containers: for example, three 500 cc water bottles. Record the amount after each bottle is finished.
Drink one cup each upon waking, after each activity, and before and after each meal. Do not drink a large amount at once.
For clients who dislike plain water, soup, unsweetened soy milk, fruit, water jelly and warm water with a little lemon all count toward fluid intake.
Constipation: Sit on the toilet 30 minutes after breakfast, with a small stool under your feet so that your knees are higher than your hips.
Massage the abdomen clockwise for 5–10 minutes daily, combined with walking or sitting/standing exercises.
Record the date and consistency of bowel movements (hard, soft, watery). Pay attention if there is no bowel movement for more than 3 days.
no: For patients with heart failure, dialysis, or fluid restriction orders, first clarify how much water they can drink daily.
Do not administer laxatives or enemas on your own; follow doctor's orders or nursing instructions.
Do not intentionally reduce water intake to avoid frequent urination.
entries.rep: If there is no bowel movement for more than 3 days accompanied by abdominal distension, vomiting, bloody stools, or black stools → report to the supervisor and recommend medical attention.
entries.ref: Independence supports the four basic cares (hydration, nutrition, exercise, and defecation).
entries.ask: The client only drinks 500 cc a day, how to design a drinking water reminder method that he can do?

entries.s: Before tube feeding, raise the head of the bed, check the tube's external markings and fixation, and check gastric residuals by aspiration as directed; keep the person sitting up for 30–60 minutes afterward.
entries.why: Tube feeding may be performed by appropriately trained home care workers, but incorrect positioning and feeding speed can cause accidents. Feeding through a displaced tube may deliver feed directly into the lungs.
steps: Before tube feeding: raise the head of the bed 30–45 degrees. Check that the tube's external marking is unchanged and that its fixation at the nostril is secure.

Follow the service provider's procedure for aspirating to check gastric residual volume. If it exceeds the provider's threshold (commonly 100–150 cc), pause and report to the supervisor; do not decide on your own.
Use feed close to body temperature and let it flow slowly by gravity. Each feeding should take at least 15–20 minutes; do not force it through.
After filling, rinse the pipe with 30-50 cc of warm water and cover the mouth of the pipe.
After tube feeding, keep the person sitting or the head of the bed elevated for 30–60 minutes before helping them turn.
If coughing, rapid breathing or a change in complexion occurs during tube feeding, stop immediately.
no: Do not give tube feeds while the person is lying flat.
If the external tube marking differs from usual, or the tube is coiled in the mouth, do not give a feed. Report first.
Do not replace a detached nasogastric tube yourself.
Do not mix medication directly with formula in the same syringe.
entries.rep: Excessive gastric residuals, a displaced or dislodged tube, or coughing/choking during feeding: stop immediately and notify the supervisor. A dislodged tube must be replaced by a nurse or medical professional.
entries.ref: Taiwan long-term care benefits and payment standard BA04: assistance with eating or tube feeding (relevant training required); the provider's tube-feeding procedure.
entries.ask: The patient often suffers from abdominal distension after nasogastric tube feeding. In addition to slowing down, what other reasons can be checked?

entries.t: Urinary catheter and drainage bag care
entries.s: The urine bag should always be lower than the bladder, the tube should not be discounted, the urethral opening should be cleaned every day, and the urine color and urine volume should be observed.
entries.why: Urinary catheters are the main source of urinary tract infections. Most infections come from the urine bag being placed too high, causing reflux, or the cleaning is not accurate.
steps: The urine bag is fixed on the edge of the bed or under the wheelchair, always lower than the bladder, and cannot be placed on the ground.
The tube is fixed on the inner thigh, leaving a little looseness. Before turning over or shifting, make sure that the tube will not be pulled.
Clean the urethral opening and the nearby catheter tubing daily using water or as instructed by the provider, working from the inner area outward.
Pour out the urine bag when it is 1/2 to 2/3 full, and do not let the outlet touch the container.
Observe and record: urine color (dark yellow, turbidity, hematuria), urine output (less than 500 cc a day should be noted), and whether there is precipitation.
no: Do not hang the urine bag above the bed or above the body for convenience.
Do not flush the bladder or remove or replace the urinary catheter by yourself.
Do not wait for the next shift when the client complains of abdominal distension and pain and has not urinated for 8 hours.
entries.rep: Turbid urine with a peculiar smell combined with fever, hematuria, anuria for more than 6-8 hours, or tube detachment → Notify the supervisor and ask for home care or medical treatment.
entries.ref: Taiwan long-term care benefit and payment standards for tube and catheter care; home nursing guidelines for urinary catheter care.
entries.ask: The patient's urine bag showed light red urine today, but he did not have a fever. What should I observe first and then report it?

entries.t: Changing diapers and protecting skin from incontinence
entries.s: Change when wet, clean from front to back, dry before wearing; do not use prickly heat powder for red rashes.
entries.why: Urine and feces on the skin for more than 1 hour will destroy keratin, and incontinence dermatitis and pressure injuries often occur together.
steps: Prepare diapers, wet wipes or warm water, dry towels, and isolation cream before starting, and try not to leave during the process.
Untie the diaper and clean it from front to back (urethra → anus) with warm water or alcohol-free wipes. For women, separate the labia to clean the folds.
Turn sideways to clean the buttocks and anus while looking at the skin of the sacrum and buttocks.
Dry completely and apply zinc oxide or skin barrier cream in a thin layer, do not apply thickly.
The size of the diaper should be correct, the waist tape should not be too tight, and the groin should be tight enough to fit one finger.
Record the frequency and characteristics of urination and defecation.
no: Do not use prickly heat powder, it will agglomerate and rub the skin when wet.
Do not use wipes with alcohol or fragrance.
Do not let the client wait wet to save diapers.
Do not open the entire diaper at once to expose the client for too long, pay attention to warmth and privacy.
entries.rep: Skin breakdown, blisters, fungal infection-like rash (small satellite-like red spots on the edge), bloody stools → Notify the supervisor.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards Basic body cleansing and excretion assistance related items; Incontinence dermatitis prevention principles.
entries.ask: The patient has recurring red rashes on his perineum. I have wiped them dry every time. Are there any other reasons that can be checked?

entries.t: Boundaries and methods for medication assistance
entries.s: Resident staff can remind, take medicine, and confirm to take it; they cannot decide the dosage, stop medicine, or give over-the-counter medicine on their own.
entries.why: Elderly people often take a variety of medicines at the same time. It is a very common abnormal event to miss taking medicine, take it repeatedly, and take the wrong medicine for family members.
steps: Before taking the medicine, confirm: the right person, the right medicine (medicine bag name), the right dose, the right time, and the right method.

If the medicine is packed in a medicine box or medicine bag, the medicine will only be given according to the contents packed by the pharmacist or nurse, and the medicine will not be opened by oneself.
Watch the patient swallow the medicine and drink enough water (those with difficulty swallowing should grind the medicine into powder or change the dosage form as instructed).
Record the medication time; if the patient refuses to take it, record and report, do not force-fed.
Pay attention to drug side effects: dizziness, drowsiness, unsteady walking, and increased risk of falling.
no: Don't judge by yourself "If your blood pressure is normal today, you don't need to take blood pressure medicine."
Do not give the client your own or family members' patent medicines or traditional Chinese medicines.
Do not mix powdered medicine into the whole bowl of rice so that the client will miss the medicine before finishing the meal.
entries.rep: If repeated use of medication, missed medication more than once, or suspected side effects are found → notify the supervisor and recommend that family members return for a follow-up visit or pharmacist consultation.
entries.ref: Pharmaceutical Affairs Law and Physician Law: Non-medical personnel are not allowed to perform dispensing and prescriptions; long-term care benefits and payment standards: medication reminders for basic daily care.
entries.ask: The client had 8 kinds of medicines in the morning, and his family members poured them all into a jar. How should I help organize them safely?

entries.t: Measuring vital signs and recognizing abnormal values
entries.s: Rest for 5 minutes before taking the measurement, and keep the cuff in position; blood pressure ≥180/110 or <90/60, blood sugar <70 or >300, and body temperature ≥38°C must be reported.
entries.why: Numbers alone will not save people, only understanding the numbers and knowing "when to report" will.
steps: Blood pressure: sit and rest for 5 minutes, with your arm at the same height as your heart, and the lower edge of the cuff 2-3 cm above the cubital fossa; if there is a big difference between the two times, measure it again.
Pulse: Count for 1 minute, watch for irregularities; watch out for <50 or >120 per minute.
Body temperature: ear temperature or forehead temperature, the same patient should be fixed in the same way; ≥38°C is a fever, and the elderly should pay attention to temperatures above 37.5°C.
Blood sugar: measure before or after meals as indicated, record time; <70 mg/dL treat hypoglycemia immediately, >300 report.
Blood oxygen: SpO₂ <92% or more than 3% lower than usual. Report if combined with shortness of breath.
The date, time and value are recorded every time, and the patient's symptoms are recorded when abnormal.
no: Do not measure immediately after the client has just moved around, drank coffee, or taken a shower.
Do not take blood pressure on the arm with an arteriovenous fistula (kidney dialysis) or breast cancer surgery.
Don't just remember the numbers and not the symptoms.
entries.rep: Blood pressure ≥180/110 or combined with headache and chest tightness, <90/60 combined with dizziness; heartbeat <50 or >120; blood sugar <70 or >300; fever; blood oxygen <92% → notify supervision; direct 119 for changes in consciousness, chest pain, and difficulty breathing.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA03 measurement of vital signs; home blood pressure measurement method of Taiwan Hypertension Treatment Guidelines.
entries.ask: The patient's blood pressure is 160/95 every time, but he does not feel uncomfortable. How often should I record it and how should I report it to the supervisor?

entries.t: Communicating with older adults with dementia
entries.s: Get into his world first and then bring him out: no corrections, no arguments, short sentences, one thing at a time.
entries.why: The memory of a person with dementia will disappear, but the emotions will remain. He may forget what you say, but he will remember it no matter how you say it.
steps: Approach from the front, call your name first, introduce yourself, keep your eyes level, wait for him to see you before speaking.
One message per sentence, use affirmative sentences: "Let's drink water" rather than "Do you want to drink water?"
Break down "what to do" into small steps to demonstrate, and give him time to react (wait 10 seconds before saying it again, don't change the words).
When what he said is inconsistent with the facts, respond to his feelings instead of correcting the content: "You miss your mother very much, right?"
When emotional, leave for a while, move to something he likes, and then come back.
Use his familiar names, old songs, and old objects to establish a sense of security.
no: Don't say "you just asked" or "you remembered it wrong".
Do not tap him from behind or touch him suddenly.
Do not discuss his condition with his family members in front of him as if he does not exist.
Do not use imperative sentences or childish tone.
entries.rep: Behavior suddenly deteriorates in a short period of time (obvious confusion, lethargy, and refusal to eat within a few days) → it may be delirium or infection, notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
entries.ref: Taiwan Dementia Association Care Manual; Ministry of Health and Welfare Dementia Care Service Principles.
entries.ask: The client says he wants to "go home" every afternoon (actually he is at home). What sentences can I use to respond?

entries.s: First find the cause (pain, urination, hunger, boredom, too noisy), then adjust the environment and work and rest, and finally comfort.
entries.why: Most of the "problem behaviors" of a person with dementia are needs that cannot be expressed in words, and behavior is his language.
steps: Eliminate physical causes when it occurs: pain, wanting to go to the toilet, hunger, too hot or too cold, constipation, drug side effects.
Sundowner Syndrome: Turn on the lights at home after 3 pm, close the curtains, reduce TV noise, and arrange regular evening activities (folding clothes, listening to old songs).
Wandering: Make sure there is a safety device on the door, have contact information on your body (love bracelet, tag inside clothing), and arrange enough activities and sunbathing during the day.
Rejection (bathing, eating, changing clothes): Change the time, change the person, change the statement, and use the order he is familiar with.
Record the time when the behavior occurred, what happened before and after, and what you did that was effective, and give it to the supervisor and family members.
no: Do not use room locks or belts to deal with wandering.
Do not argue or force him as this will increase aggression.
Don't keep pushing him while he's eating or bathing.
entries.rep: Lost once, injured due to aggressive behavior, or continues to refuse to eat for more than one day → notify the supervisor; if lost, call the police immediately and notify family members.
entries.ref: Dementia Care Guidelines of the Ministry of Health and Welfare; Article 51 of the Elderly Welfare Law (Prohibition of interfering with the freedom of the elderly and leaving them in dangerous environments).
entries.ask: The client has to go out to "go to work" after 8 pm, and his family members are already very tired. What methods can I suggest that do not require restraint?

entries.t: Checking the home for fall hazards
entries.s: Every time you arrive at the home, scan around it with your eyes: floor, light, circulation, shoes, bathroom, bed height.
entries.why: More than half of the falls at home occur in the moving line from the bathroom and bedroom to the toilet. Residential staff are the people who can best detect dangers.
steps: Floor: Small carpets, wires, sundries, and slippery places should be removed or fixed; thresholds can be equipped with ramps.
Light: At night, a moving line and a night light are provided, and there is a light that can be turned on easily by the bed.
Movement line: The path from the bed to the toilet is clear, and there are fixed objects that can be supported along the way (not folding chairs or movable tables).
Bathroom: non-slip mats, handrails, shower chairs, handrails or booster seats next to the toilet.
Shoes: Heel covered, soles non-slip, no slippers for walking.
Bed and chair height: When sitting down, your feet should be flat and your knees should be at about 90 degrees.
If you see a danger, correct it on the spot if you can (move the wire). If you cannot change it, record it and report it.
no: Do not ask the client to reduce walking for fear of falling, as muscle strength will decrease and the patient will fall more severely.
Do not let the patient go to the toilet by himself when he has just gotten up after taking sleeping pills or blood pressure lowering drugs.
entries.rep: The client has fallen in the past 3 months, walks obviously unsteadily, and needs to hold on to the wall to walk → Notify the supervisor and recommend referral for home rehabilitation or assistive device evaluation.
entries.ref: The Ministry of Health and Welfare's guidance on fall prevention for the elderly; long-term care assistive devices and home accessibility improvement services.
entries.ask: My family’s bathroom does not have handrails and they are unwilling to install them. What are some cheap or temporary alternatives?

entries.s: Restraint is a medical behavior and requires medical advice and family consent; the resident staff does not take the initiative to restrain, and should report improper restraint.
entries.why: Studies have repeatedly proven that restraints do not reduce falls, but instead increase the risk of muscle weakness, pressure injuries, delirium and death.
steps: Find the reason first: Is extubation because of itching or discomfort? Is the restlessness due to pain or wanting to go to the toilet?
Alternative methods: distracting items (towels, pillows), sitting where you can see people, regular activities to consume energy.
The line can be covered with clothing, fixed more securely, or asked to be evaluated by a nurse to see if it can be removed.
Use low beds, floor mats, and bedside sensors instead of bed rails and straps around the bed.
When you see family members restraining themselves, first understand the reasons, explain the risks, and report to the supervisor for handling.
no: Do not "protect" the client by tying his hands, tying his feet, tying him to a chair, or locking him in a room.
Do not pull up all sides of the bedrail (it will cause the bedrail to climb over and fall more seriously).
entries.rep: It is found that the client has been restrained for a long time, has strangulation marks or skin injuries, and is locked in the room → handle according to the reporting responsibility, report to the supervisor and 113.
entries.ref: The principle of dignified care in the Long-term Care Services Act; Article 51 of the Elderly Welfare Act; Article 75 of the Act on the Protection of the Rights and Interests of Persons with Disabilities.
entries.ask: The family members tied the client to the bed because they were afraid that he would fall in the middle of the night. How should I discuss alternatives with the family members?

entries.s: Oral suction is limited to the mouth, in front of the uvula, and requires completed training. Each suction attempt must last no longer than 10 seconds; provide oxygen or rest before and afterward as described in the original.
entries.why: Oral suction can reduce choking, but if the suction is too deep or too long, it will cause hypoxia or damage the mucosa; endotracheal suction belongs to another item and training.
steps: Confirm that you have completed the provider-approved training and that this procedure is included in this person’s approved care services.
Wash hands, the client sits up or lies with his head turned to one side, and prepares a suction machine, sterile sputum suction tube, and clean water.
Insert the suction catheter only into the mouth, no farther than the uvula. Apply suction while rotating and withdrawing it, for no more than 10 seconds each time.
Let the patient rest, take a deep breath, and observe the complexion and blood oxygen between the two suctions.
After suctioning, clean the tubing and mouth. Record the color and amount of secretions and the person’s response.
no: Do not extend the oral suction tube deep into the throat or nasal cavity.
Do not continue pumping when the patient's face turns purple and his blood oxygen drops.
Do not execute without training and approval.
entries.rep: The secretion is yellow-green, bloody, the amount suddenly increases, and the blood oxygen does not rise after pumping → notify the supervisor or 119.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA18 Suction of secretions in the mouth (before the uvula) (training required); BA17 Suction of secretions in the artificial airway tube are otherwise regulated.
entries.ask: The client has a lot of phlegm but cannot extract it with oral suction. What other care practices can be taken to make it easier to cough up the phlegm?

entries.t: Four foundations of reablement and independence
entries.s: Water 1500 cc, nutrition, exercise, regular bowel movements - take good care of your physical condition first, then you can develop your functions.
entries.why: Many "reluctances to move" are actually caused by dehydration, malnutrition, and constipation, which makes people weak and lack of energy. Take care of the basics first, then exercise will be effective.
steps: Moisture: Approximately 1500 cc of water per day if prescribed by a physician, measured in a visible container.

Nutrition: Each meal has protein (eggs, tofu, fish, meat), about 1-1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day; if the teeth are not good, change the protein to soft instead of reducing the amount.
Exercise: There are opportunities to stand up, walk around, and do things by hand every day. It is not "just lying down and resting".
Defecation: Sit on the toilet at a fixed time and record defecation.
Write these four things into the daily service record so that the supervisor and family members can see the changes.
no: Don't use "the client doesn't want to move" as the reason for closing the case. Ask first if the patient's physical condition is insufficient.
Don't do everything for convenience, leaving the client with no chance to exert force all day long.
entries.rep: Obvious inability to eat, weight loss, and drinking less than 1000 cc of water within two weeks → Notify the supervisor and recommend nutritional or medical evaluation.
entries.ref: The four basic care principles of independent support care; the principles of long-term care rehabilitation services.
entries.ask: The client weighs 72 kg, has bad teeth, and only eats porridge. How should he supplement his protein every day? Please give me the specific menu.

entries.t: Learning by doing: three stages of support without taking over
entries.s: Give oral prompts first, then demonstrate or gesture, and finally assist with hands, and only assist the section that cannot be done.
entries.why: Working on behalf of others is the fastest, but every time you work on behalf of others, the client will practice one less time; rehabilitation is to turn daily life activities into training.
steps: Ask yourself first: Which part of this action can the client do and which part cannot he do?
First paragraph: spoken prompts ("Hands on the handrails" "Buttocks forward"), wait 10 seconds.
The second paragraph: Demonstrate or touch the part to be moved as a prompt.
The third paragraph: Only help with the part that cannot be done (such as buttoning the top button), and let him do the rest by himself.
After completion, specifically praise the part that was done: "You stood up three times today!"
Changes in level of assistance (full assistance → partial assistance → verbal prompts) were recorded.
no: Don't act while the client is still trying.
Don’t finish everything every time due to time pressure; you can discuss adjusting the service period with your supervisor.
entries.rep: The client's ability has significantly improved or declined → report to the supervisor as a basis for service plan adjustment.
entries.ref: Long-term care rehabilitation service concept: life is rehabilitation, learning by doing.
entries.ask: The client needs my help every time he puts on pants. Please help me break down putting on pants into small steps and find out the parts that he can do by himself.

entries.s: Plant your feet firmly, lean forward, push your knees to stand up, and sit down slowly; 10 times x 3 times a day is the most effective lower limb muscle strength training.
entries.why: Sit-stand is a key action for "whether you can go to the toilet by yourself"; the number of sit-stands in 30 seconds is a common physical fitness indicator for the elderly around the world.
steps: Use a chair with a backrest that will not slip, and the height should be about 90 degrees for the knees; do not place a table in front of the chair.
Feet shoulder-width apart, heels slightly pulled back; nose over toes (lean forward).
Stand up with your hands on your thighs or cross your chest; if you can't do this, hold on to the armrests of the chair or stabilize the tabletop in front of you.
Stand up straight, pause for 2 seconds, then take 3–4 seconds to sit down slowly without "falling" into the chair.
8-10 times at a time, rest for 1 minute, do 2-3 times; at least 3 days a week.
Advanced: holding hands without support, holding water bottle, lowering chair.
no: Do not use wheels or folding chairs.
Do not do it when the client is dizzy or has unstable blood pressure.
Don't let the client hold his breath and exert force. Exhale when standing up.
entries.rep: Chest pain, obvious breathlessness, dizziness, severe knee pain during exercise → Stop and handle according to exercise safety indicators.
entries.ref: 30-second sit-to-stand test (Senior Fitness Test); muscle strength training guidelines for the elderly.
entries.ask: The client can only sit and stand 3 times with support. Please help me design a 4-week progressive plan.

entries.t: Seated leg raises and ankle pumps
entries.s: Sit and straighten your calf for 3 seconds, and stretch your ankle up and down to prevent muscle strength decline and calf blood clots.
entries.why: The quadriceps muscles of the elderly who sit for a long time will degenerate first and the blood circulation of the calves will become poor. There are almost no taboos in these two actions and they can be done while sitting.
steps: Sit firmly on the chair, lean back well, and hold the chair surface with both hands.
Slowly straighten one foot, hook the toes toward yourself, pause for 3 seconds and then put it down; alternate 10 times with both feet.
Ankle pump: Hook the toes of both feet upward for 2 seconds, then push down for 2 seconds, do 20 times.
Advanced: Tie sandbags or elastic bands around your ankles.
2-3 times a day, you can do it while watching TV or waiting for meals.
no: Do not lift your legs when the knee has just been operated on or is acutely swollen and painful.
Don't hold your breath.
entries.rep: Sudden swelling, pain, heat and redness of one side of the calf → it may be a blood clot, notify the supervisor and recommend immediate medical treatment.
entries.ref: Home exercise guidelines for the elderly; Principles of deep vein thrombosis prevention.
entries.ask: The client has edema in both feet. What are other safe home practices besides leg lifts and ankle pumps?

entries.t: Upper limb exercises with a towel
entries.s: Use a towel to stretch, twist, lift, and pull your back to exercise shoulder, arm and hand strength, and dress and bathe accordingly.
entries.why: Putting on and taking off tops, washing your hair, and wiping your back all require shoulder joint mobility and grip strength. Towels are a training tool that every household has.
steps: Grasp both ends of the towel with both hands and pull it tightly to both sides, raise it to the top of your head and then lower it, 10 times.
Put the towel behind your back and pull it up and down (like wiping your back), interchange your hands up and down, 10 times each.
Twist the towel: twist your hands in opposite directions 10 times to practice grip strength and forearms.
Tighten the towel with both hands and push forward and pull toward the chest, 10 times.
Advanced: Wet the towel and add weight.
no: If you have acute shoulder pain or frozen shoulder, do not lift until it hurts.
Don't shrug your shoulders and relax your neck.
entries.rep: Pain during shoulder movement for more than two weeks and waking up with pain at night → Notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
entries.ref: Upper limb functional training and ADL corresponding principles for the elderly.
entries.ask: The client cannot lift his right shoulder to his ear, and it is very difficult to put on a jumper. Please suggest 3 corresponding towel movements and dressing techniques.

entries.s: Hold the back of the chair with both hands → one hand → release your hand and practice standing balance; the key point is "there are things you can grab but try not to grab them".
entries.why: Balance is the most direct indicator of fall risk and will improve after just 2–3 weeks of practice.
steps: Stand behind a stable chair with your hands on the back of the chair and your feet shoulder-width apart for 30 seconds.
Stand with feet together for 30 seconds.
Stand with one foot in front and one foot behind (heel to toe) for 30 seconds, then switch feet.
One-legged stance: Lift one foot off the ground for 5–10 seconds, switch feet, 5 times each.
After each level is done steadily, you can advance to one-hand support and then let go of the hand (the hand is still placed 5 centimeters above the back of the chair and is on standby).
There must be someone next to you.
no: Do not do it on slippery ground or wearing slippers.
Do not do it when the patient has just taken sleeping pills or antihypertensive drugs or is dizzy.
Don't jump through several difficulty levels at once.
entries.rep: Can’t stand on one leg for less than 5 seconds and has fallen in the past 3 months → Notify the supervisor and recommend referral for rehabilitation assessment.
entries.ref: Otago exercise program balance training principles; Taiwan elderly fall prevention exercise guidelines.
entries.ask: The client will wobble when standing with his feet together. Please help me list the order of balance exercises starting from the simplest.

entries.t: Walking practice and mobility aid checks
entries.s: First check the height and anti-slip of the assistive device, then start from a short distance indoors, and use "walk together" instead of "walk with support".
entries.why: Many elderly people are not unable to walk, but the height of the assistive devices is wrong, the anti-slip pads are worn flat, or the caregivers keep using them so that they lose their balance.
steps: Crutches/walkers height: When the hand is hanging down naturally, the handle is at the wrist crease, and the elbow is slightly bent at about 15-30 degrees when holding it.
Check whether the anti-slip foot pads are smoothed and whether the screws are loose.
Walking aid: push out one step first → affected foot → good side foot; hold crutches in the good side hand.
You walk behind the client's affected side, put your hands on the back of his waist without grabbing it, and let him control his balance.
Starting from 5-10 meters indoors, accumulating every day, the target can walk to the toilet, dining table, and door.
Wear covered shoes and record the distance walked every day and whether you stopped to rest.
no: Do not use armrests to pull you around.
Do not start out outdoors or on uneven surfaces.
Do not let the client use an umbrella or broom instead of a cane.
entries.rep: Suddenly becomes obviously unsteady when walking, has unilateral weakness, or becomes breathless after walking a few steps → Notify the supervisor and recommend medical evaluation.
entries.ref: Principles of assistive device use; long-term rehabilitation walking training.
entries.ask: The patient's walking aid was purchased online by his family. How can we help him quickly confirm whether the height is correct?

entries.s: The mantra "good up, bad down": when going upstairs, the good foot goes first, and when going downstairs, the bad foot comes first; the crutches follow the bad foot.
entries.why: Stairs are the place where the consequences of falling at home are most serious. If the order is correct, the risk will be reduced by half.
steps: Going upstairs: Holding the handrail, the good foot goes up first, followed by the bad foot and crutches, one step at a time.
Going downstairs: go down with the crutch and the bad foot first, then the good heel.
You stand one step below the client (at the back when going upstairs and in front when going downstairs), with your hands behind your waist.
Threshold: stand firm first, raise your feet and step over without dragging your feet; a ramp can be installed.
Only take the steps within your ability range at a time, and you can rest in the middle.
no: Don’t be distracted by chatting while walking.
Do not carry the client up and down the stairs (two people fall together).
Do not wear slippers or go up and down stairs barefoot.
entries.rep: Unable to go up and down stairs safely, resulting in inability to go out for medical treatment → Notify the supervisor and evaluate stair-climbing machines or transportation resources.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA12 Assistance in going up and down stairs; principles of rehabilitation walking training.
entries.ask: There are five stairs without handrails at the door of the client's house. His left foot is weak. How can I help him get out safely?

entries.t: Bridging and independent turning in bed
entries.s: You can also practice while lying down: hip lift bridge pose, grabbing the bed rail to turn over, sitting up on the bed, which is the first step to leave the bed.
entries.why: Muscle strength will drop by 10 to 20% after a week of bed rest. Exercise in bed is to give him the strength to sit up and get out of bed.
steps: Bridge pose: Bend your knees and step on the bed, lift your buttocks off the bed, hold for 3 seconds, and put it down, 10 times; you can start by lifting 1 centimeter.
Turn over on your own: Pull the bed rail in the direction you want to turn over, bend your knees on the other side and push in the same direction, you only assist your shoulders.
Sit up in bed: lie on your side → support the bed with your hands → put your feet down on the edge of the bed, divided into three steps, and wait for him to use his own strength for each step.
After sitting on the edge of the bed, place your feet on the ground and sit for 3-5 minutes to see if you feel dizzy before doing any sitting exercises.
The time of sitting on the edge of the bed is gradually extended every day.
no: Do not perform a bridge friction wound when there is a sacral pressure injury.
Do not pull the client's arm to sit up.
Do not leave when you first sit up, be aware of postural hypotension.
entries.rep: Severe dizziness when sitting up, blood pressure drops by more than 20 mmHg, or the client is completely unable to participate → Report to the supervisor for assessment of reinstatement intervention.
entries.ref: Long-term rehabilitation bed activity training; Principles of prevention of postural hypotension.
entries.ask: The client has been bedridden for three months, and his family members want him to go out in a wheelchair. Please help me plan a four-week gradual plan from bed exercises to sitting on the edge of the bed.

entries.s: Do each joint slowly to the end, pause for 3 seconds, and do it 10 times. Do not exceed the pain point; if you can move by yourself, do not do it passively.
entries.why: Joints will contract if they are immobile for more than a few weeks. After contracture, changing diapers and dressing are more difficult and painful.
steps: Sequence: shoulder (lift, abduction), elbow (flexion and extension), wrist (up and down), fingers (grip and release), hip (flexion, abduction), knee (flexion and extension), ankle (hook and extension).
Fix the proximal end of the joint with one hand and support the distal end with one hand, slowly reach the maximum range he can do, and stop for 3 seconds.
Each action is performed 10 times, 1-2 times a day; ask him to do it by himself if he can do it (active exercise), and you only help where he can't do it.
Watch your expression while doing it. If you frown or cry out in pain, step back a little.
Record which joints become less mobile or tighter.
no: Do not swing quickly or press hard to the bottom.
The fracture is not healed, the joint is acutely red, swollen, hot and painful, and the surgical site is not treated immediately.
Do not perform vigorous passive exercises on patients with severe osteoporosis.
entries.rep: The joint suddenly becomes hard and swollen, and there is severe pain during movement → notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment; the contracture progresses rapidly → it is recommended to refer for reinstatement.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA11 Limb joint movement; principle of passive joint movement.
entries.ask: After the patient suffered a stroke, his left fingers were clenched and unable to be opened. What should be paid attention to when doing finger ROM and how to make him relax?

entries.s: The formula "put on the affected side first, then take off"; use sitting position, loose clothing, and devil's felt instead of buttons, and let the client complete it by himself.
entries.why: Dressing is an action that must be done every day, and it is an upper limb and balance training in itself.
steps: Sit firmly on the edge of a chair or bed, with clothes spread out and face up on your lap.
Coat: Put the hand on the affected side first into the sleeve and pull it to the shoulder, then put on the good side; when taking it off, take off the good side first.
Pants: When sitting, put the affected foot into the trouser leg first, then put on the good side, pull it to the knee, stand up and then pull it to the waist.
The buttons are difficult: change to devil felt, large buttons, and elastic trousers; the shoelaces are difficult: change to elastic shoelaces.
You only assist if he is stuck for more than 10 seconds, and only assist on the step where he is stuck.
no: Don't put the whole outfit on for him just to be quick.
Do not let him put on his pants while standing (unless well balanced and with handrails).
entries.rep: Repeatedly falling down when dressing or the need for assistance increases significantly → Report to supervision.
entries.ref: Occupational therapy ADL training principles; long-term rehabilitation functional training for daily life.
entries.ask: The client's right hand is hemiplegic and he has been failing to wear a zippered coat. Please give me a breakdown of the steps and two improved methods.

entries.s: Adjust the tableware, plate, height and time, and let the patient put the meal into his mouth by himself, with you just assisting.
entries.why: Eating by yourself is not only about dignity, but also training in hand-eye coordination, upper limb muscle strength and swallowing.
steps: Sitting posture: The height of the dining table is about a little above the navel, and the feet can touch the ground.
Cutlery: thick-grip spoons, non-slip placemats, rimmed plates (non-spill plates), light cups.
Cut vegetables into bite-size pieces and use wide-mouthed bowls for soup to reduce the frustration of not being able to scoop it out.
Hand shaking or weakness: Hold his hand and bring it to your mouth (hand in hand), slowly reduce your strength.
Given enough time, a meal of 30–40 minutes is normal.
Record the proportion (how many percent) that can eat by itself.
no: Don't feed it directly just because it eats slowly and sheds a lot.
Don't clean up when he's in the middle of eating, it will interrupt the rhythm.
entries.rep: Significant reduction in food intake, coughing, and weight loss → Notify the supervisor.
entries.ref: Occupational therapy feeding training and assistive device principles.
entries.ask: The client has Parkinson's disease and his hands are shaking and he often spills food when eating. What are some cheap tableware or improvement methods?

entries.s: From "regular reminder" to "walking to the toilet by yourself", use the toilet booster seat and handrails to reduce the time of wearing diapers.
entries.why: Being able to go to the toilet by oneself is the independent ability that the elderly care about most, and it is also the rehabilitation goal that can best reduce diaper and skin problems.
steps: First record the time of urination for 3 days and find the pattern (for example, every 2 hours).
Take the initiative to remind you to go to the toilet 15 minutes before the regular time, do not wait for him to shout.
Toilet: booster seat, side armrests; bedside potty chair available at night.
The clothing is changed to elastic pants for easy and quick removal.
From you accompanying → you waiting outside the door → going by yourself, gradually reducing assistance.
Try using pant diapers or cotton pads instead of adhesive diapers during the day to give him the motivation to "go by himself".
no: Don’t wear diapers all day and limit drinking water just because you are afraid of incontinence.
Don't let him hold his urine until you are free.
entries.rep: Painful urination, hematuria, frequent urination combined with fever, sudden inability to urinate → notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA24 Assistance with excretion; independence support excretion care principle.
entries.ask: The client wears diapers during the day but can actually walk. Please help me design a two-week toilet training schedule and record sheet.

entries.s: Do this 5 minutes before meals: take a deep breath, stretch your neck, inflate your cheeks, stretch your tongue, and pronounce "lay, he, ka, la".
entries.why: Swallowing muscles will also degenerate. Doing oral exercises before meals can reduce choking, increase saliva, and improve eating safety.
steps: Take 3 deep breaths and raise and lower your shoulders 5 times.
Turn your neck left and right, and bend your neck left and right 5 times each (do it slowly).
Pump your cheeks and inhale alternately 5 times; open your mouth wide and say "Ah" and close your mouth tightly "Hmm" 5 times.
Extend the tongue, retract it, and press the cheek on the left and right sides 5 times each.
Pronunciation: "Bapapapa, he-he-he, kakaka, la la la" 5 times each, clearly and powerfully.
Finally coughed 2 times and swallowed saliva 1 time.
no: Do not perform neck movements after acute neck pain or cervical spine surgery.
Don't get dizzy.
entries.rep: Even after doing oral exercises, he still chokes repeatedly, drools more, and his voice becomes hoarse → Notify the supervisor to recommend speech therapy evaluation.
entries.ref: Japanese Oral Gymnastics; Taiwan Elderly Oral Function Promotion Program.
entries.ask: Please adapt the calisthenics into a version to the rhythm of an old Taiwanese song, suitable for a group of 10 people.

entries.s: Nostalgic chatting, simple arithmetic, finding things, sorting and organizing, hide cognitive training in daily affairs.
entries.why: The most effective form of cognitive stimulation is "meaningful and interactive" rather than doing questions.
steps: Nostalgia: Use old photos, old songs, and old objects to start the topic, and ask "at that time..." instead of asking him "who is this".
Counting: getting change when buying groceries, counting how many pills there are, and counting how many glasses of water you drank today.
Classification and organization: fold clothes into colors, pair socks, organize drawers.
Find things: Put 3 items on the table, cover them, take one away, and ask what is missing.
Board games: poker card matching, big dice ratio, simple picture card matching.
15-20 minutes each time, on the principle that the client has a smile and is willing to continue.
no: Do not use an "examination" tone or correct mistakes.
Don’t choose activities that are too difficult to frustrate him, rather be simple but have a sense of accomplishment.
entries.rep: Cognition worsens significantly within a few weeks → Notify supervisor to recommend medical evaluation.
entries.ref: Principles of cognitive stimulation therapy (CST); guidelines for non-pharmacological interventions in dementia.
entries.ask: The client has mild dementia and used to be a tailor. Please design 5 home cognitive activities related to her occupation.

entries.t: Pre-exercise checks and signs to stop
entries.s: Check blood pressure, symptoms, and environment before exercise; stop immediately if chest pain, obvious breathlessness, dizziness, or pale face occur during exercise.
entries.why: Sports safety is not about "don't move", it is about knowing which situations you cannot move today and which situations you should stop immediately.
steps: Confirmation before exercise: resting blood pressure <160/100, no fever, no chest tightness, slept last night, and eaten today.
Environment: Wear covered shoes, the ground is dry, there is something stable to hold on to, and there is water next to it.
Warm up for 5 minutes first (stepping in place, mobilizing joints).
During exercise, ask "Are you okay?" every few minutes and check your face and breathing.
Stop immediately: chest pain and tightness, difficulty breathing and unable to speak complete sentences, dizziness, pale face and cold sweat, chaotic heartbeat, severe joint pain.
After stopping, sit down and rest for 10 minutes. If the symptoms do not disappear, follow the emergency procedures.
no: Do not exercise on the day when blood pressure ≥180/110, wheezing, fever, blood sugar <70 or >300 when resting.
Do not hold your breath and exert force (blood pressure will soar).
entries.rep: Stop indicators appear during exercise and do not improve with rest, or they occur every time you exercise → Notify the supervisor, and it is recommended to seek medical evaluation before continuing.
entries.ref: ACSM Exercise Safety Guidelines; Taiwan Elderly Exercise Prescription Principles.
entries.ask: The client has a history of heart stent installation, and his family members are very worried. Please list the exercises he can do safely and the situations that must be avoided.

entries.s: If you can talk but can't sing, it's just the right medium intensity; if you can't speak a complete sentence, it's too strong.
entries.why: Without instruments at home, the conversation test is the simplest and most accurate strength judgment.
steps: During the exercise, ask the client to say a sentence, such as "The weather is very good today and I want to go out for a walk."
Can finish a sentence smoothly → medium intensity, just right.
Panting while speaking, can only speak three or four words → too strong, slow down.
Can sing → too light, you can speed up or increase the number of times.
Perceived exertion level (0-10): Aim for 4-6 "a little tired but can continue".
Record the intensity of each exercise.
no: Don't rush the client with "it's effective when you're tired".
Don't use young people's heartbeat standards.
entries.rep: Breathing or chest tightness below moderate intensity → Notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
entries.ref: Talk Test; Borg Perceived Exertion Scale.
entries.ask: Please write a paragraph to explain to the 80-year-old client what "just the right amount of exercise intensity" is in the most vernacular way.

entries.s: Abdominal breathing and pursed-mouth exhalation, 10 times each, 2 times a day, can make patients who are bedridden or have poor lung function breathe more efficiently.
entries.why: Bed rest, hunchback, and lung disease will all make breathing shallow, phlegm cannot be coughed out, and pneumonia can easily occur.
steps: In a semi-sitting or sitting position, place one hand on your chest and the other on your stomach.
Inhale slowly through your nose for 3 seconds and feel your belly bulge (without moving your hands on your chest).
Pout your lips like blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for 4–6 seconds.
Do 10 breaks, 2–3 times a day.
When there is phlegm: After taking a deep breath, cough hard 2 times (a breathy cough), and then pat the back (hollow palm from bottom to top).
Advanced: Blowing balloons, blowing bubbles, blowing water with a straw.
no: Don't get dizzy.
No patting on the back after just eating.
Do not do it when blood oxygen is low or short of breath, report first.
entries.rep: Respiration rate per minute >24, blood oxygen <92%, sputum with blood or yellow-green color combined with fever → notify supervisor or 119.
entries.ref: Pulmonary recovery breathing training principles; long-term care benefits and payment standards BA10 Turn over and pat the back.
entries.ask: The client has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and gets breathless after walking a few steps. Please help me design a combination of breathing and exercise that can be done while sitting.

entries.t: Six steps for responding to an incident
entries.s: Safety → Disposal → Report → Record → Handover → Review. If there is any abnormality, please ensure the safety of the scene before making a call.
entries.why: When in a panic, it is most likely to miss "ensure safety first" and "record that day". These two things often determine subsequent responsibilities and the outcome of the case.
steps: Ensure safety: both yourself and the client are out of danger (fire, gas, water on the ground, out-of-control people).
Preliminary treatment: handle according to the approach of each incident; if life is in danger, call 119 directly, do not ask the supervisor first.
Report: Immediately notify the supervisor by phone (not just send a message), and notify family members in accordance with unit regulations; 110/113 when necessary.
Recording: Complete the day's record before leaving the client's home. Use 5W1H to write facts, not speculation.
Handover: Inform the next class or family members of the matters and time points that need to be continued observation.
Review: Discuss the causes and preventive measures with the supervisor, and fill in the abnormal event notification form according to the unit's time limit (mostly within 24 hours).
no: Do not delay reporting or downplay the facts for fear of being blamed.
Do not promise compensation or apologize to family members in private.
Do not post client photo discussions in LINE groups.
entries.rep: Any falls, injuries, medical emergencies, lost encounters, suspected mistreatment, injuries to the attendant, sexual harassment/violence must be reported.
entries.ref: Regulations on reporting of abnormal events in units; service quality and reporting specifications of the Long-term Care Services Act.
entries.ask: (Describe the incident) just happened to me at home. Please help me compile an objective draft report record in accordance with 5W1H.

entries.s: Time, place, person, what happened, what you did, the client’s situation and the person to whom you report - only write the facts you saw and heard.
entries.why: Records are your most important self-protection and the only basis for subsequent medical treatment and investigation.
steps: When: At what time it was discovered or occurred (not approximately).
Where: living room, bathroom, bedside - specific location.
Who: The client, the family members present, you.
What: Objective description "The client was found sitting on the floor in the bathroom, with the right side of his body on the ground, pain in his right hip, and clear consciousness."
How/Disposal: What did you do, who was notified at what time, how the other party responded, and the follow-up status of the case owner.
Quotes from the client or family members are recorded in the original text in quotation marks. For example, the client said, "I slipped on my own."
Signature, date, and submit to supervisor; keep a summary of the record for yourself.
no: Do not write speculations such as "should be" or "maybe because".
Do not use emotional words ("The family members are very fierce" is changed to "The family members raised their voices and said...").
Do not post-date records with incorrect dates.
entries.rep: After the record is completed, it shall be handed over to the supervisor; when legal matters are involved, the record shall be kept by the unit.
entries.ref: Principles of writing service records; the evidentiary value of written records in civil litigation.
entries.ask: Please rewrite this spoken description into an objective record of abnormal events, removing speculation and emotional words: (paste the content).

entries.s: Do not help immediately. First ask if you can move, see if there is any deformation or bleeding, or if your head has been hit, and then decide to help him up or call 119.
entries.why: Rushing to get up after falling is the main cause of fracture displacement and secondary injuries; the mortality rate of the elderly with hip fractures is very high within one year.
steps: Ask the client not to move first, squat down and talk to him: "Don't get up in a hurry, let me take a look first."

Check: Is the consciousness clear? Where does it hurt? Can your feet move? Are both feet the same length (one foot is turned out and shortened → suspected hip fracture)? Is there any bleeding, deformation, or head impact?
Any of the following: unconsciousness, severe pain, inability to move, deformation, vomiting or drowsiness after head impact, heavy bleeding → Do not help, call 119, keep warm and accompany.
None → Let the client turn over, kneel up, hold on to something solid and stand slowly while you are there to protect him; do not use a puller.
After lifting, sit down and rest for 15 minutes, then measure blood pressure and observe.
Notify the supervisor and family members, and record the cause, location, and injury of the fall; continue to pay attention to headache, vomiting, and changes in consciousness within 24 hours.
no: Do not pick up or lift by arms.
Don’t fail to report just because the client says “it’s okay”.
Do not move a client with suspected cervical spine or hip injury.
entries.rep: Report all falls to supervisor; 119 if injured or unsure. Head impactors are observed for 24–72 hours.
entries.ref: Ministry of Health and Welfare's guidelines for fall prevention and fall management in the elderly; unit fall reporting standards.
entries.ask: After the patient fell, he said he was fine, but his right foot was obviously shortened and turned outward when walking. How should I describe the situation to 119?

entries.s: Vomiting, drowsiness, severe headache, unilateral weakness, and pupils of different sizes within 72 hours after hitting the head → 119.
entries.why: Symptoms of cerebral hemorrhage in the elderly may appear hours to days after hitting the head, especially in those taking anticoagulant drugs.
steps: First confirm whether there are any immediate danger signs: unconsciousness, convulsions, bleeding or clear water from ears and nose, pupils of different sizes → 119.
Trauma treatment: Use clean gauze to compress scalp bleeding, and apply ice for 15 minutes if it becomes swollen.
Confirm whether you are taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs (such as warfarin, aspirin) → inform the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
Observation focus for family and next shift handover: Monitor sobriety every 2–4 hours for 72 hours.
Occurrence: repeated vomiting, increasing sleepiness and difficulty waking up, worsening headache, unclear speech, unilateral weakness of hands and feet, and unsteady walking → 119.
no: Do not give painkillers to mask symptoms.
Do not let the client sleep alone all night without anyone watching.
entries.rep: All head impacts must be reported to the supervisor; if there are signs of danger, report immediately 119.
entries.ref: Guidelines for home observation of head trauma; risk of bleeding with anticoagulants.
entries.ask: The client hit his head and is taking anticoagulant drugs. His family members do not want to be sent to the hospital. How can I explain the risks?

entries.s: Apply direct pressure to stop bleeding for 10 minutes without letting go; unable to hold back, bleeding spurting, deep or large wound → 119.
entries.why: The elderly have thin skin and often take anticoagulant drugs, and minor injuries may bleed for a long time; correct compression is the only effective way to stop bleeding.
steps: Wear gloves (to protect you and him).
Use clean gauze or towel to press directly on the wound, and continue to press for 10 minutes without opening it all the time.
Compress while raising the injured area above the heart (when there is no fracture).
When blood oozes out, add another layer to cover it. Do not remove the original one.
After the small wound has stopped bleeding, rinse it with physiological saline or water and cover it with a clean dressing.
Record the amount of bleeding (estimated), wound size and treatment.
no: Do not use a tourniquet, powder or toothpaste.
Do not apply cotton directly to the wound.
Do not remove foreign objects inserted into the body by yourself.
entries.rep: If the pressure does not stop after 10 minutes, spurt-like bleeding, fat visible in deep wounds, animal bites, wounds on the face or joints → 119 or seek medical attention; otherwise report to supervision.
entries.ref: Basic first aid principles; Article 14-2 of the Emergency Medical Assistance Act exempts good-faith first aid.
entries.ask: The patient's skin is very thin, and the skin will bleed when the tape is torn off. Please suggest a suitable fixation and dressing method.

entries.s: Rinse the blisters and cover them: Rinse with running cold water for 15-30 minutes, take off clothes carefully, do not break the blisters, cover with a clean cloth, and send to the doctor.
tags: Rinse off the bubble cap and send it
entries.why: Elderly people have thin skin, and they will be scalded if they soak in water at 40 degrees Celsius for a long time; the length of flushing time determines the depth.
steps: Flush: Flush the injured area with running cold water (not ice water) for 15-30 minutes until it no longer hurts.
Take off: Carefully take off your clothes in the water. Cut off the sticky parts, do not tear them.
Soak: Continue to soak in cold water. Elderly people with large area burns should pay attention to hypothermia. Do not soak for too long if the body surface area exceeds 10%.
Cover: Cover lightly with a clean damp cloth or plastic wrap, do not wrap tightly.
Send: The area is larger than the palm, face, joints, perineum, large blisters appear or the skin becomes white and zoom → 119.
Record the cause of burns (such as hot water bottle, bath water temperature) and review prevention.
no: Do not apply toothpaste, soy sauce, ointment, or ice cubes.
Do not pop blisters.
Do not rub the injured area vigorously.
entries.rep: All burns are notified to the supervisor; those who meet the medical standards are 119.
entries.ref: Taiwan Ministry of Health and Welfare burn first-aid mnemonic: cool with running water, remove clothing, soak, cover, and seek medical care.
entries.ask: The client used an electric blanket to sleep, which caused redness and swelling in the calf without breaking the skin. How should I deal with and prevent it?

entries.s: If the person can cough, encourage coughing. If they cannot cough or speak and turn blue, perform abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled. If they collapse, switch to CPR and call 119.
entries.why: It only takes a few minutes from the occurrence of choking to hypoxia in the elderly, and you are the first line.
steps: First ask "Are you choking?" Can cough and speak → Encourage to cough hard without patting on the back.
Completely unable to cough, unable to make a sound, grabbing throat with both hands, and turning purple → Immediately perform abdominal pushing.
Stand behind the person with one foot in front of the other. Make a fist and place it two finger-widths above the navel. Grasp the fist with the other hand and thrust quickly inward and upward.
Push repeatedly until the foreign body is discharged or the client loses consciousness.
Loss of consciousness → Let him lie down, beat 119 (or ask someone else to beat him), and start CPR; before each blow, check whether there is any foreign object in the mouth that can be removed.
After discharge, the supervisor should still be notified and medical treatment recommended (there may be internal organ injury).
no: Do not blindly dig your throat with your fingers.
Do not pat the back (it will make the object deeper).
People in wheelchairs who cannot stand: can do abdominal pushing from behind on a chair, or chest pushing for pregnant or obese people.
entries.rep: Report all choking incidents to supervisor; lose consciousness or remain unwell after being pushed → 119.
entries.ref: Taiwan First Aid Guidelines for Choking Treatment; Emergency Medical Assistance Act Article 14-2.
entries.ask: The client is in a wheelchair and I am present alone. He choked. Please tell me step by step how to do abdominal pushing.

entries.s: If you have a crooked face, droopy hands, or unclear speech, if one of these appears, call 119 and write down the "last normal time".
entries.why: Stroke treatment is time-critical. Each additional hour of delay can increase disability. The time the person was last known to be well helps determine eligibility for thrombolytic treatment.
steps: F face: Ask the client to smile and see if the corners of the mouth on both sides are symmetrical.
Hand A: Close your eyes and raise your hands flat for 10 seconds to see if one hand droops.
S Speak: Ask him to speak a word and see if he is unclear or answers questions incorrectly.
T Time: Any abnormality → Call 119 immediately, say "suspected stroke", and tell the ambulance what time the patient was last seen.
During the waiting period: let the client lie on his side or half sit, do not give food and water, do not give medication, keep the respiratory tract unobstructed, and record the changes in symptoms.
Notify the supervisor and family members, and prepare the medication list and health insurance card.
no: Don't "watch it first to see if it's okay."
Do not drive yourself to the hospital (the ambulance can go directly to a hospital with stroke treatment capabilities).
Do not give water or medicine (swallowing may have been affected).
entries.rep: For any positive FAST sign, call 119 immediately, then notify the supervisor.
entries.ref: Taiwan Stroke Association FAST identification formula; emergency medical rescue method.
entries.ask: The client suddenly became weak on one side of his hand but recovered after ten minutes. He said there was no need to call an ambulance. What should I do?

entries.s: Blood sugar <70 or sweating, trembling hands, palpitations, confusion: give 15 grams of sugar if conscious, and then measure again after 15 minutes; 119 if unconscious.
entries.why: The original explains that low blood glucose can be more dangerous than high blood glucose and may cause coma within tens of minutes. A common cause at home is receiving insulin without eating.
steps: Symptoms: cold sweats, trembling hands, fast heartbeat, dizziness, sudden tantrums or answering questions that are inappropriate, and drowsiness.
If there is a blood glucose machine, measure immediately; if there is no blood glucose machine but the symptoms are obvious, treat it as hypoglycemia first.
If conscious and able to swallow, give 15 grams of sugar: 3 sugar cubes, 150 cc of sugar-containing juice or soda, or 1 tablespoon of honey. Do not use sugar-free products or artificial sweeteners.
Recheck after 15 minutes. If the value is still <70, give another portion. Once it rises, provide a starchy snack such as crackers or bread.
If consciousness is impaired, the person cannot swallow, or they are convulsing, do not give anything by mouth. Place them on their side and call 119.
Notify the supervisor and family. Record the time, glucose reading and what was given. Look into possible causes, such as a missed meal, medication amount or excessive activity.
no: Do not feed sugar water when you are unconscious (you will choke).
Do not give chocolate (more fat is absorbed slowly).
Do not let the client sleep alone after handling the case. Someone should observe him.
entries.rep: Report all hypoglycemia events to supervision; unconsciousness or recurrence → 119/Recommended follow-up for medication adjustment.
entries.ref: Diabetes Health Council 15 Rules for Managing Hypoglycemia.
entries.ask: The client has diabetes and difficulty swallowing. What safe sugary foods can be used when hypoglycemia occurs?

entries.s: Chest pain that lasts for more than 5 minutes, cold sweats, pain in the shoulders and jaw, or wheezing when resting → Direct 119, do not seek medical attention yourself.
entries.why: Elderly people with myocardial infarction often "just feel chest tightness, nausea, and very tired", and the symptoms are atypical; waiting is myocardial necrosis.
steps: Ask the client to stop moving, sit in a semi-sitting position (do not lie down if you have difficulty breathing), and loosen the collar and waistband.
Observe: location of chest pain, how long it lasts, cold sweats, nausea, purple lips, and whether you can breathe while talking.

Any of the following → 119: Chest pain that lasts for more than 5 minutes or does not improve with rest, pain to left shoulder/chin/back, cold sweat, shortness of breath and inability to speak complete sentences, blood oxygen <90%.
If the person has physician-prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin and their blood pressure is not low, assist with use according to the medical order.
Stay with the person while waiting, measure blood pressure and prepare the medication list. Do not give food.
If unconscious and not breathing → CPR.
no: Do not allow the client to walk to the toilet or go up and down stairs by himself.
Don't procrastinate by "laying down first."
Do not self-administer painkillers or family members' heart medications.
entries.rep: Directly 119, then notify the supervisor and family members.
entries.ref: Myocardial Infarction First Aid Guidelines; Emergency Medical Care Act.
entries.ask: The client has a history of heart disease. Today he said "he feels tight in his chest and feels a little nauseous" but refuses to call an ambulance. What can I do?

entries.s: Do not suppress or put things in your mouth; remove dangerous objects and record the time; more than 5 minutes or the first attack → 119.
entries.why: The attack itself usually lasts for a few minutes, but the real danger is bruising, choking, and lasting more than 5 minutes.
steps: Look at the clock and note the start time.
Move away things that may hit you, put something soft under your head, and loosen your collar.
Do not suppress, do not stuff, do not give water or medicine.
After the convulsions stop, let him lie on his side (resuscitation position), clear his mouth, and keep his airway open.
Watch the person as they regain awareness. They will often be tired and confused. Stay with them; do not leave them alone.
Seizures lasting more than 5 minutes, consecutive attacks, first attack, still not awake 15 minutes after attack, injury, difficulty breathing → 119.
no: Do not attempt to open the mouth or insert a spoon.
Do not hold down the limbs with force.
Do not move the client during a seizure (unless in a dangerous location).
entries.rep: All convulsions are reported to supervision; those who meet the requirements 119.
entries.ref: Taiwan Epilepsy Medical Association Seizure Management Principles.
entries.ask: The client has a history of epilepsy. After the attack, he is very confused and wants to get up and walk. How can I accompany him safely?
