steps: Take about 45 cm of dental floss and wrap both ends around the middle fingers of both hands, leaving 3–5 cm in the middle.
Use your thumb and index finger to support it, and pull the saw back and forth to gently slide it into the gap between the teeth without "bounce" it in.
Curve the dental floss into a C shape against the tooth surface, and scrape upward toward the gums 2-3 times; repeat on the other side of the tooth surface.
Use a piece of clean floss every time you open a gap between teeth.
It is difficult to operate the back teeth or the patient’s hands are not flexible: use a dental floss stick (Y-shaped is better) or use an interdental brush.
Rinse mouth after use and observe for bleeding.
no: Do not press too hard into the gums.
Use a floss threader or interdental brush under the denture fixed bridge without hard pulling.
Do not share floss picks with clients.
entries.rep: The dental floss gets stuck or breaks in the same place every time, and the gums continue to bleed → Dental advice is recommended.
entries.ref: National Oral Health Guidelines of the Ministry of Health and Welfare.
entries.ask: The patient has large gaps between his teeth and has periodontal disease. Which one is more suitable, flossing or interdental brushing? How to choose size?

entries.s: Choose a size according to the size of the gap between your teeth (it can be easily put in, and a little resistance is just right). After moistening it, gently move it in and out 2-3 times horizontally, once a day. Rinse and dry after use.
entries.why: The interdental brush is the most practical interdental cleaning tool for the elderly: it is easier to operate than dental floss and is suitable for large gaps between teeth, periodontal disease, dental implants and fixed dentures.
steps: Choose the size: Start with the smallest size, which can be easily inserted and the bristles contact the tooth surfaces on both sides. If it is too tight, change to a smaller size. The same mouth may need two sizes.
Apply damp (maybe a small amount of fluoride toothpaste or mouthwash), do not brush dry.
Put it into the gap between the teeth from the edge of the gum level, gently move it back and forth 2-3 times, do not rotate or force it.
Back teeth: Bend the metal rod of the interdental brush into an L shape for better operation, or choose an angled style.
Once a day, preferably before brushing your teeth in the evening.
Rinse clean after use, spin dry, and hang upright; replace the bristles if they are deformed or the metal is exposed.
no: Do not shoehorn an interdental brush that is not the right size (it can damage your gums, crush the metal rod and puncture it).
Do not share it with more than one person.
If there is bleeding, continue to use it gently for a week. If bleeding still occurs, dental surgery is recommended.
entries.rep: Continuous bleeding, swelling, pain, and pus between teeth → Dentistry is recommended.
entries.ref: Ministry of Health and Welfare National Oral Health Guidelines; Periodontal Disease Care Principles.
entries.ask: The client has dental implants and fixed dentures. How to use interdental brushes and which areas need to be cleaned in particular?

entries.t: Hair washing while seated or in bed
entries.s: The water temperature is 38-40℃, protect your ears and eyes first, keep fingernails off your fingertips, wash and dry quickly; those who are bedridden should use a shampoo sink or basin, and blow dry within 5 minutes after washing.
entries.why: Scalp oil and sweat can cause itching and folliculitis, but hair washing is the most common cleaning item for the elderly to catch colds and dizziness.
steps: Preparation: 2–3 towels, shampoo, water bottle or shower head, earplugs or cotton balls, hair dryer, close the window to keep warm.

Sitting position (bathroom): Sit on a bathing chair, tilt your head slightly forward, protect your forehead and eyes with one hand, and rush forward from back to avoid water entering your eyes and ears.
On the bed: Put a tarpaulin and towel under your shoulders, put your head in a shampoo tank or inflatable shampoo basin, ear plugs and cotton balls, and put a water bucket under the bed.
Wash: Rinse first and then use shampoo. Use your fingertips to make circular motions to massage your scalp without scratching with your nails; rinse until there is no foam.
Dry: Press the towel to absorb water, and blow dry within 5 minutes (keep the hair dryer 15 cm away and do not stay in the same place). Check the scalp for wounds, rashes, and head lice.
The whole process was controlled within 10 minutes, during which time I was asked if I felt dizzy or cold.
no: Do not raise your head to flush for too long (dizziness, cervical discomfort).
Do not pour hot water directly on your head.
Do not wash when you have just eaten or when your blood pressure is unstable.
Don't leave with wet hair.
entries.rep: Scalp wounds, large rashes, head lice, obvious dizziness when washing hair → Notify supervisor.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA23 assists in washing hair, BA07 assists in bathing and washing hair; care attendant training: hair cleaning.
entries.ask: The client is bedridden, his cervical spine cannot be tilted back, and there is no hair washing sink at home. What are some alternative ways to wash hair in bed?

entries.s: Wash one area at a time and cover it immediately after washing, in the order of face→arms→chest and abdomen→back→legs→perineum, change the water 2-3 times, the whole process takes 15-20 minutes.
entries.why: The skin of bedridden people is cleaned by scrubbing and bathing. If done well, it can prevent pressure injuries and infections. If not done well, it will cause hypothermia and loss of dignity after being exposed for too long.
steps: Prepare: two basins of warm water (38–40°C), two towels (one for wiping and one for drying), bath towel, lotion, clean clothes, close the windows and draw the curtains.
Take off your clothes to expose only the parts to be washed, and cover the rest with a bath towel.

Sequence: eyes (from the inner corners of the eyes outward, one eye at a time) → face → ears and neck → arms (from far to near) → armpits → chest and abdomen (the folds under the breasts of women should be wiped dry) → back and buttocks (turn sideways and look at the skin at the same time) → legs and feet → perineum and finally.
Dry each area immediately and cover it back; change the towel if it is dirty or the water is dirty.
When rubbing your back, you can pat or massage it gently to promote circulation. Look at the sacrum and shoulder blades.
Apply lotion to dry areas; keep dry between toes and creases.
Put on clean clothes, make sheets, and change wet sheets.
no: Don't strip off completely and then start rubbing.
Don’t use a towel from head to toe.
Do not rub hard on areas with thin skin.
Clients with pipes should be careful not to pull on the pipes.
entries.rep: New erythema, blisters, broken skin, and unknown bruises are found → notify the supervisor.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA01 Basic body cleanliness; care attendant training: bed wiping and bathing.
entries.ask: The client is in bed and is very afraid of the cold. He keeps shivering when taking a shower. Please give me a way to keep warm and shorten the process.

entries.s: Wear gloves, wipe from front to back, from inside to outside, and change faces; women separate the labia, and men remove the foreskin, clean it, and then push it back; explain before taking action, and respect privacy.
entries.why: Perineal cleaning done well is the most important step in preventing urinary tract infection. It is also the most sensitive and shameful care for the client; skills are as important as attitude.
steps: Preparation: gloves, warm water, alcohol-free wipes or gauze, dry towel, close the curtain and expose only the perineum.
Let me explain first: "I will help you clean it now, it will be a little cold."

Women: Lie on your back with your knees bent and your legs apart. Use one hand to separate the labia, and use the other hand to wipe the inner thighs with wet gauze from the front (urethral opening) to the back (anus), changing sides after wiping without going back and forth.

Males: Hold the penis with one hand, pull back the foreskin to expose the glans, clean from the urethral opening outward, rinse or wipe it clean and push the foreskin back to its original position (very important, otherwise it will become swollen and incarcerated); then clean the scrotum and groin.
Anus: Turn sideways and wipe from front to back to see if there are hemorrhoids or broken skin.
Wipe dry, observe secretions, odor, redness, swelling, and broken skin. If you have a urinary catheter, clean the urethral opening and the proximal end of the tube.
Arrange clothes, take off gloves and wash hands, record abnormalities.
no: Do not wipe from back to front (bringing anal bacteria to the urethra).
Men should not forget to push the foreskin back after cleaning.
Do not clean mucous membranes directly with soap or alcohol-based wipes.
Do not proceed without curtains in the presence of family members or others.
entries.rep: Abnormal discharge with odor, redness, swelling, broken skin, inability to push back the foreskin, and painful urination → Notify the supervisor and recommend medical treatment.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA01 basic body cleanliness, BA24 assistance with excretion; care attendant training: perineal cleaning.
entries.ask: The client is a male and I am a female housekeeper. He is very resistant to perineal cleaning. What methods can be used to reduce the embarrassment of both parties?

entries.t: Assisted joint movement: technique and sequence
entries.s: Fix the upper part of the joint with one hand and support the lower part with the other hand, slowly, steadily, to the bottom, and stop for 3 seconds; from the proximal end to the distal end, 5-10 times in each direction, depending on the expression, not the number of times.
entries.why: It is also a "moving joint". The position and speed of the hand rest determine whether to help him or hurt him. (For a list of training exercises, please see the "Joint Mobility Exercises" in the rehabilitation database.)
steps: Warm first: You can apply warm towel or massage gently to relax the muscles before moving.
Grip method: Hold both ends of the joint, do not grasp the joint, do not grasp the fingertips; touch the entire surface of the palm, do not pinch with the fingertips.
Speed: One movement lasts 3-5 seconds to the end, pauses for 3 seconds, and comes back again in 3-5 seconds; no bounce, no fast swing.
Sequence: shoulder → elbow → wrist → fingers; hip → knee → ankle → toes. 5–10 times in each direction.
Hemiplegic side: When moving the shoulder joint, support the upper arm to avoid dislocation. Do not just pull the wrist and raise it.
Watch the expression and muscle tension while doing it. If you frown or resist, step back a little and slow down.
When you are done, return to a comfortable position and note which joints are tight or painful.
no: Do not force a joint beyond its reach.
Do not do this if the fracture has not healed, the joint is acutely red or swollen, or the area has just been operated on.
Do not force it when the client resists or the spasm intensifies.
entries.rep: Joint swelling and pain, significantly reduced range of motion, and contracture progression → Notify the supervisor and recommend referral for rehabilitation.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA11 Limb joint movement; care attendant training: joint movement.
entries.ask: After the patient had a stroke, the tension in his arms was very high and became tighter when he moved. What should he do to prevent spasms when moving the joints?

entries.t: Transfer boards, slide sheets and two-person transfers
entries.s: Clients who are completely unable to bear weight, are heavy, or have pipelines use a shift board/sliding mat/two-person method without holding; use the same command and exert force at the same time to protect their waist.
entries.why: One person’s back injury is the number one cause of back injury among home staff, and the client will also be injured if his armpit is grabbed or his skin is pulled. With the right tools, one person can complete it safely.
steps: Judgment: The client can stand with support → use a standing transfer; cannot stand but can sit firmly → shift board; cannot sit firmly and stay in bed → sliding mat or two-person method (or lift).

Shifting board (bed↔wheelchair): Both are of the same height. The wheelchair has the armrests locked and braked. One end of the board is placed under the patient’s buttocks and the other end is placed on the seat of the wheelchair. The client leans forward. You hold the belt and let him move over step by step.

Sliding mat (move up or turn over on the bed): Place the sliding mat under the body. Two people stand on each side and grab the edge of the sliding mat. With the command "one, two, three", they pull it toward the head or side at the same time without lifting it.

Two people shift: one person is responsible for the upper body (hands are hugged from the armpits to the chest), and the other person is responsible for the legs. At the same time, the command is given, and the knees are bent and straightened.
Your posture: feet in front of one another, close to the client, using your legs instead of your waist, and not twisting your body.
After the transfer, check the person’s sitting position and medical tubes, and document the findings.
no: Do not grab the armpits and lift them up.
Do not move a client alone who exceeds his own weight and is completely unable to bear the weight.
Do not operate the bed wheels or wheelchair without locking them.
Don't turn around and move people.
entries.rep: The patient suffers pain or falls down during the shift, and you move to the waist → Report abnormal events; repeated difficulties → It is recommended to supervise and evaluate the lift or assistive device subsidies.
entries.ref: According to the Occupational Safety and Health Act, employers should provide safe working methods; subsidies for long-term care assistive devices (shift boards, shift slides, lifts).
entries.ask: The patient weighs 90 kg and is bedridden. I am the only one at home. Please help me determine which kind of assistive device to apply for and what alternatives to apply before applying.

entries.s: Sit with your butt as low as possible, with your hips, knees and ankles at about 90 degrees, with your feet on the pedals, back-to-back pads, and your pelvis not tilted; change positions or decompress after sitting for an hour.
entries.why: A crooked sitting posture can cause sacral pressure, body slipping, spinal deformation, and also make it difficult for the client to eat and breathe.
steps: First push the buttocks to the end: let the patient lean forward, and you can hold the pelvis from behind and pull it back, or use a sliding mat.
Check the three 90 degrees: hip, knee, ankle; footrest height is such that thighs are flat and knees are no higher than hips.
The pelvis is symmetrical: the ischium on both sides presses against the cushion; a wedge-shaped cushion can be placed on the crooked side.
Back: The cushion supports the waist and the head does not hang forward.
Hemiplegic side arm: Place it on the table or pillow, do not hang next to the wheel.
Pressure reduction: Assist with forward or side tilt for 1 minute every 30–60 minutes, or use an air mattress or pressure relief cushion.
When wearing a seat belt, it is buckled on the pelvis, not the stomach; it is not a restraint, but to prevent it from slipping.
no: Do not allow the client to slide to the front edge of the seat for a long time (sacral compression).
Do not remove the footrests and leave your feet dangling.
Don't use donut cushions.
entries.rep: The erythema on the sacrum or ischium does not fade after sitting, and the patient is unstable and slips repeatedly → Notify the supervisor and recommend evaluation of assistive devices (positioning wheelchair, pressure-reducing cushion).
entries.ref: Long-term care assistive device services (wheelchair positioning accessories, pressure relief cushions); pressure injury prevention principles.
entries.ask: The patient’s wheelchair always tilts to one side and slides off after half an hour. The wheelchair at home is a normal one. How can I adjust it first?

entries.t: Boarding and leaving accessible care transport
entries.s: The lift plate of the wheelchair should be locked, face the inside of the car, and fasten the fixed belt; the patient who can walk should help him step into the car step by step, sit down first and then retract his feet; confirm the seat belt and belongings before and after getting in and out of the car.
entries.why: Getting on and off the vehicle is the moment when you are most likely to fall and be injured when going out, and it is also the action that requires the most division of labor with the driver.
steps: Reservation and confirmation: Rehabilitation bus or long-term care transportation (BD03) must be reserved in advance, and inform the wheelchair type, number of companions, destination, and whether oxygen is available.
Before departure: the client goes to the toilet, brings the health insurance card and medication list, checks the brakes and pedals of the wheelchair, and wears safe shoes.

Wheelchair lift plate: The brakes are locked, the wheelchair is facing into the car or according to the driver's instructions, you stand behind the wheelchair and hold the handles, and do not touch the edge of the lift plate when rising.
Fixation in the car: The four-point fixed belt of the wheelchair and the client's seat belt are buckled, and you sit in a position where you can see the client.

Clients who are able to walk: After holding the car door handle with one hand and supporting your waist with the other, sit in the seat first and then retract your feet (turn around and sit in); when you get off the car, put your feet on the ground first and then stand up.
Upon arrival: Confirm your belongings (crutches, medicine, health insurance card) before letting the car leave.
no: Do not release the brakes or turn the wheelchair on the lift.
Do not carry the client in and out of the vehicle.
Do not leave the client alone in the vehicle.
Do not move up or down until the vehicle is stopped and the lift plate is not leveled.
entries.rep: Injuries, pinches, and falls when getting on and off the vehicle → Report to the supervisor and family members, and record; report vehicle safety issues to the pick-up and drop-off units.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BD03 Transportation pick-up and drop-off services; Rehabilitation bus riding regulations; Operational specifications of long-term care transportation pick-up and drop-off units.
entries.ask: The client uses an electric wheelchair and needs to take a rehabilitation bus. What information should be provided when making a reservation, and what should be paid attention to when getting on the bus?

entries.s: Before departure, bring all the documents, medication list and problem list. During the consultation, assist the patient to clearly explain the main complaint and write down the medical orders, and hand them over to the family members and supervisor after returning.
entries.why: Accompanying him to medical treatment is not just about "accompanying him", but also allowing the patient's questions to be heard by the doctor and the doctor's instructions to be taken home; the resident attendant is the only bridge in the process.
steps: Before departure: health insurance card, ID card, medication list or medicine bag, past examination reports, list of questions written by family members, wheelchair or crutches, water and snacks (especially for diabetics).
Write down what you want to ask in advance: why you came this time, recent symptoms (when did they start, how often), whether you have fallen, and blood pressure and blood sugar records.

When seeing a doctor: Let the patient speak for himself first, and then add more if he can’t explain clearly; do not make treatment decisions for him, and do not sign the consent form (by his family members).
Write down the doctor's orders: new medicines, drug withdrawals, return dates, inspection items, precautions; if you don't understand, ask on the spot.
When receiving medicine, check the name and quantity in the medicine bag, and confirm with the pharmacist how to take the new medicine.

Return trip: whether the client is feeling unwell and whether he has eaten; when he returns home, inform his family members of the doctor’s orders, return date, and medication changes, record them, and report to the supervisor.
no: Do not decide for the client whether to have surgery or to be hospitalized - this is a decision for the family and the client.
Do not sign consent forms for surgery, anesthesia, etc.
Do not leave the client to do your own business while waiting for treatment.
Do not tell irrelevant people about the client’s condition.
entries.rep: If the condition worsens during medical treatment, it will be handled according to emergency procedures; important matters (hospitalization, discontinuation of medication) explained by the doctor will be reported to the supervisor and family members on the same day.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA14 Accompanying medical treatment; Regulations on signing consent forms for surgery under the Medical Law; Personal Data Protection Law.
entries.ask: The client is going to see the neurology department tomorrow. The family members only said that "he has been acting strange recently." Please help me make an observation list that can be brought to the doctor.

entries.s: Your role is a safety net and a metronome: check first before starting, demonstrate once, follow suit, count the beats, look at the expression, and stop at the right time; do not do it for him, nor force him as a coach.
entries.why: Most of the clients do not lack exercise knowledge, but they lack "someone to accompany them"; the effect of accompanying exercise comes from the relationship and rhythm, not the difficulty of the movements.
steps: Before starting: Ask about today's status (sleeping, eating, pain, medicine), take blood pressure, wear closed shoes, clear the ground, and put water next to it.
Start the show the way he likes: play old songs, chat, start with the moves he did yesterday.
Demonstrate once, and then do it together. You count the beats ("one, two, three...") and verbally prompt the key points of the action ("step firmly" and "exhale").
Check your face and ask "Are you okay" every 3-5 minutes, and stop when the stop indicator appears.
If you can do it, give specific praise ("Two more strokes today than yesterday"), if you can't do it, demote the person without force.
Ending: gentle stretches, drinking water, recording what was done, how many times, and feelings.
Treat the actions in the resuscitation database as a menu, and pick 3–4 at a time. You don’t need to complete them all.
no: Don’t “keep it up” when the client is uncomfortable.
Don't work too hard without looking at him.
Don’t use your phone to time the clock and stare at the screen without looking at the person.
entries.rep: Chest pain, obvious wheezing, dizziness, and falls during exercise → Follow the emergency and fall procedures; continue to refuse exercise → Report to the supervisor for discussion and adjustment.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA02 Basic daily care activity assistance; rehabilitation database "pre-exercise examination and cessation indicators".
entries.ask: The client said, "It's useless for me to exercise when I'm so old." Please give me three different responses to make him willing to exercise with me.

entries.s: Accompanying is not just sitting around and swiping your phone: it has a purpose (safe viewing, talking, and activities), there are observations (emotions, behaviors, environment), and there are records; when accompanying someone to go out, plan the route, resting spots, and toilets first.
entries.why: Companionship is the easiest project to make "people are present but not in the heart"; done well, it is the best time to detect abnormalities and maintain functional and emotional support.
steps: First confirm which item is approved: safe viewing (BA22, mainly for safety) or accompanying outings (BA13, including shopping, walking, and social activities). The content depends on the approval.

Accompanying at home: Arrange something to do together (folding clothes, talking about old photos, listening to the radio, playing cards), and at the same time observe the spirit, diet, and environment; do not let the client watch TV the whole time while you slide your phone next to him.
Conversation skills: open-ended questions ("What did you do this morning?"), listen attentively, don't rush to give advice, don't talk about politics, religion, and other people's rights and wrongs.

When traveling with an escort: first confirm the destination, route, mode of transportation, availability of toilets and rest points, weather and medication times; bring water, medication, health insurance card, and contact card.
When going out: walk on the weak side, cross the street and walk on zebra crossings, hold your belt lightly in crowded places, and ask if you need a break every 15–20 minutes.
After returning home: record where you went, how long you were gone, the client’s condition, and noteworthy things in the conversation (depressed mood, mention of wanting to die, conflicts at home).
no: Do not take the client to places other than approved places (your own home, crowded temple fairs) without the permission of the employer.
Do not let the client out of sight when out and about (for example, if you stop the car and let him stand on the side of the road).
Don’t agree to the client’s secret request of “not telling the family members”. Tell them first and you will report back in accordance with the regulations.
entries.rep: During the conversation, the client expressed that he wanted to die, be abused, and have his property taken away → notify the supervisor on the same day (the 1925 reassurance hotline is also provided for thoughts of death); falling or getting lost while outing should follow the abnormal event process.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA13 accompanied outings, BA22 safe viewing; unit standards for accompanied outings.
entries.ask: The client lives alone and seldom speaks. I have two hours of companionship every week. Please design companion activities that are not repeated for four weeks and do not require materials.

entries.t: Preparing meals together: reablement in the kitchen
entries.s: Break down meal preparation into steps that can be done while sitting down (wash vegetables, peel garlic, beat eggs, arrange dishes) and give them to the client. You are responsible for the fire and knife; the goal is that he can prepare a meal for himself.
entries.why: Preparing meals while practicing hand finesse, standing endurance, sequential memory and decision-making is the most complete daily training, and the results can be eaten.
steps: First divide the work: What does the client do (deciding the dishes, washing the vegetables, peeling, tearing, stirring, and plating), and what do you do (turn on the fire, cut, and heat the pot).
Set standing endurance: Start with sitting and increase the time you spend standing at the sink each week (1→3→5 minutes).
Cognition: Ask the client to tell the sequence of steps, find the required utensils, and calculate the portions (how many eggs, how many cups of rice).

Hands: If the dominant hand is weak, use anti-slip pads to fix the bowl and tools with large handles; hemiplegic patients use the affected hand to press the ingredients and operate on the better side.
Safety: put away the knives immediately after use, turn the gas on and off by you, and have a stable support next to the client when standing.
Record which extra step he did this week.
no: Don’t do everything just for him to “see” for the sake of efficiency.
Don't let him stand alone before the fire.
entries.rep: Repeatedly forgetting steps during meal preparation, causing burns and cuts → report to supervisor for assessment of awareness and safety.
entries.ref: Long-term care rehabilitation service life function training; BA05 meal care.
entries.ask: The client used to be good at cooking, but now she has mild dementia and often forgets the steps. Please help me design a "division of work schedule" for a dish so that she can participate 80%.

entries.s: Start by going to the alley to buy something: walking endurance, looking for goods, counting money, paying, taking it home, and push forward a little bit every week.
entries.why: Shopping includes walking, recognizing, counting, speaking, and lifting. It is the most life-oriented multi-task training and the starting point for rebuilding social participation.
steps: Week 1: Walk to the nearest store together, buy only one thing, and you pay; record how many minutes you walked back and forth and how many times you took a break.
Week 2: Let the client find the product by himself and get it to the counter.
Week 3: Let the client count the money and pay by himself (use cash first, counting coins is cognitive training).
Week 4: Let the client carry a bag of light things home (lifting heavy objects to train upper limbs and balance).
Advanced: Increase the distance, add more items, change a store, and write your own list.
Check shoes, weather, water and resting spots before going out every time.
no: Don’t go to a big box store in the first place (too far, too noisy, too many choices).
Don't rush to help the client while he's counting money, wait.
entries.rep: Significant decrease in walking endurance, extreme fatigue after going out, or falling → Report to supervision.
entries.ref: Long-term care rehabilitation service community participation training; BA13 accompanying outings.
entries.ask: The client has not been out for three months after his stroke. Please help me design a gradual outing plan from the doorstep of his home to the convenience store.

entries.s: Divide brushing into holding a toothbrush → squeezing toothpaste → brushing → gargling → putting them back, find out the steps he can do, use a modified handle and a fixed sequence, and practice twice a day.
entries.why: Brushing one's own teeth is one of the easiest self-care skills to restore, has two opportunities to practice every day, and directly reduces the risk of pneumonia.
steps: Observe first: At which step is he stuck? Unable to hold it firmly (grip strength), unable to squeeze out toothpaste (coordination of both hands), unable to brush on one side (neglect or out of hand), forgetting the sequence (cognition).
Grip strength: Make the toothbrush handle thicker (cover it with a foam tube, wrap it with a towel), or change it to an electric toothbrush.
Coordination of both hands: Change the toothpaste to push type, or you can squeeze it first.
Unable to swipe: Demonstrate in front of the mirror, or gently guide his hand to that side (hand-in-hand), and then slowly release it.
Sequence: Paste a picture next to the mirror (upper right → upper left → lower left → lower right → tongue).
You only need to brush the areas that he can't brush, don't brush the whole mouth again.
no: Don't take over the whole thing just because he didn't clean it well.
Don't ask to do it all yourself at once.
entries.rep: Oral condition worsens (bleeding, bad breath, ulcers) → Notify supervisor and recommend dentistry.
entries.ref: Occupational Therapy ADL Training; Department of Health and Welfare Oral Health Guidelines.
entries.ask: The client has hemiplegia in his right hand and inflexible left hand. Please give me three assistive devices and training steps for him to brush his teeth by himself.

entries.s: From the front door to the alley, to the bus stop, to taking the bus at one stop; what I practice is the change of road surface, crossing the road, getting on and off the bus and the balance in the crowd.
entries.why: Walking well indoors does not mean walking well outside: slopes, sidewalk height differences, green light seconds, and bus braking are all new challenges.
steps: The first level: from the front door of your home to the alleyway, back and forth, recording the time and number of breaks.
Second level: Add height differences (sidewalks, thresholds) and slopes; practice "stop first, look, then step over".
The third level: Crossing the road - start when the light turns green, walk on the zebra crossing, and watch the signal for seconds in the middle.

The fourth level: Go to the bus stop and wait for the bus, get on the bus (grasp the handrail first and then lift your feet), sit firmly, ring the bell, and get off the bus (wait for the bus to stop, feet first, then body).
At each level, you can do it without your support and the client is not nervous before moving on to the next level.
The weather, physical strength, and medication time must all be coordinated.
no: Don’t pick rush hours in the first place.
Don’t look at the navigation on your phone while walking.
Don’t let the client leave the reach of your hands in a crowded place.
entries.rep: Falls while walking outdoors, obvious fear and dare not go out again → Report to supervision and evaluate assistive devices or psychological support.
entries.ref: Community participation in long-term care rehabilitation services; BA13 accompanying outings.
entries.ask: The client wants to resume taking the bus to the market by himself. Currently he can walk at home for 10 minutes. Please help me plan the six-week training phase and the passing standards for each level.

entries.t: A client goes missing during an outing
entries.s: If you find that the child is missing, immediately search around the place for 5-10 minutes, and call the supervisor and family members at the same time; if you cannot find the child, immediately call the police 110 (people with dementia do not have to wait 24 hours), and provide photos and clothing.
entries.why: The first hour after being lost is the most critical; a person with dementia will not wait for you where you are, and the later the delay, the greater the range of the alarm.
steps: Immediately stop what you are doing, first look in the most likely direction (toilet, exit, a road he is familiar with, heading home), and call his name.
Ask shop staff or passers-by to help look out for the missing person. If they are not found within 5–10 minutes, stop searching on your own.

Call 110 to report the crime: name, age, height and build, clothing, last seen time and place, whether you have dementia, whether you have a mobile phone or a love bracelet; the police can assist in the search immediately.
Notify the supervisor and family members, and family members can notify the dementia assistance system and relatives and friends at the same time.
Stay near the last seen location and wait for the police and family members. Do not drive around by yourself.

After finding the person, check for injuries and dehydration, and record the entire process; review with the supervisor afterwards (anti-lost measures before going out: contact cards, GPS, holding hands).
no: Don't delay calling the police thinking "he'll be back soon".
Don’t hide or fail to report.
Do not blame the client.
entries.rep: 110 (immediately) → Supervision → Family members; fill in the abnormal event report afterwards.
entries.ref: The Police Department assists in the search for missing persons (people with dementia can be accepted immediately); regulations for company accompanying people when going out.
entries.ask: I accompanied the client with dementia to the market, and when I turned around he disappeared. Please tell me in chronological order what I should do at each step in the first 15 minutes.

entries.t: Deterioration or injury during appointments or outings
entries.s: In the hospital: find the nearest nursing station or ring the emergency bell; on the road: stop, sit down or lie down, determine whether it is 119, notify the supervisor and family members at the same time, and do not force yourself to send him home.
entries.why: When you go out without a blood pressure monitor or family members, there is only one criterion for judgment: Would I call 119 in this situation at home? If you can, just fight.
steps: In the hospital: Immediately call for the nearest medical assistance (nursing station, waiting area volunteers, emergency department), do not wait for the original outpatient clinic.
On the road or in the car: Have the client sit or lie down, loosen the collar, and observe consciousness, breathing, and face.
Meets emergency conditions (chest pain, difficulty breathing, altered consciousness, positive FAST, unable to stand after falling, massive bleeding) → 119, state the location clearly.
Not applicable but feeling unwell → Rest nearby, replenish fluids, contact family members to decide whether to seek medical treatment instead, and do not continue the trip reluctantly.
Notify the supervisor, accompany family members or when ambulance arrives, and hand over the medication list to the ambulance crew.
Record time, symptoms, treatment, and notification targets.
no: Do not decide to take the person home first and deal with the problem later.
Do not leave the client alone to find someone.
Do not hail a car to the emergency department yourself (unless 119 is unreachable).
entries.rep: 119 → Supervision → Family members.
entries.ref: Emergency Medical Assistance Act; long-term care benefits and payment standards BA13, BA14.
entries.ask: When I was waiting with the client in the hospital, he suddenly broke into a cold sweat and said he felt dizzy. Who should I call and what should I say at the scene?

entries.t: Kitchen incidents: cuts, pan fires and gas left on
entries.s: Use direct pressure to stop bleeding if a cut is made; cover the pan if it is on fire, turn off the heat and never pour water; do not turn on electrical appliances if you smell gas, open the window, turn off the main switch, and leave before calling 119.
entries.why: Meal preparation is something that housekeepers do every day, but the kitchen is the place where most accidents occur at home.
steps: Cut: Wear gloves and clean gauze to apply direct pressure for 10 minutes, then elevate; if it is deep or cannot be pressed → seek medical advice.

Oil pan catches fire: Turn off the heat, cover with a pot lid or a large sliding lid, and move away from the fire source; do not splash water or move the pot; cannot cover it → take the client away, close the door, 119.
Gas smell: Do not touch any switch or ignition. Open the window and turn off the main gas switch. Take the client out of the house and call 119 and the gas company.
For burns, please "rinse off the bubble cap and send it away".
Post-event review: Whether anti-scalding gloves, timers, gas interrupters, and induction cookers are needed instead.
Report to supervisor and record.
no: Do not pour water on the pan.
Do not turn on the range hood or light when there is a smell of gas.
If the client has a history of dementia or forgetting to turn off the fire, do not let him use the gas stove alone.
entries.rep: Fire and gas → 119; Injury → Seek medical treatment according to the injury and notify the supervisor.
entries.ref: Fire Department Fire Protection Guidelines for Homes; Principles of First Aid for Burns and Scalds.
entries.ask: The client often forgets to turn off the gas. What safety equipment can I recommend to the family? How to apply or purchase?

entries.t: Disputes over shopping costs or change
entries.s: Take out the invoice and check it item by item with the record, speak calmly, and don’t argue; if you don’t agree or the client insists on being short-changed, ask the supervisor to intervene immediately, and don’t make up the money yourself.
entries.why: If the amount dispute is not handled well, it will turn into a "theft accusation"; only by having records and supervision in the middle can both parties be protected.
steps: First ask the client or family members to sit down and spread out the invoices, goods and records to check them one by one.
The client remembers incorrectly (common in dementia): explain gently, do not overcorrect, and ask family members to help confirm.
It’s really not right: honestly explain the possible reasons (missing an invoice, the store made a mistake), report it to the supervisor on the same day, and let the unit handle it.
Record the content of the dispute, the statements of both parties, and the verification results.
Precautions afterward: Count the money in person before and after going out, ask the client to sign or confirm with family members, and take photos of the invoices and save them in the unit system.
no: Do not pay the difference out of your own pocket (which is equivalent to admitting it).
Don't use an accusatory tone of voice like "You remember it wrong."
Don’t hand over an invoice without retaining it.
entries.rep: Supervision; if it turns into a theft charge, it will be handled according to the legal database "Accused of stealing or damaging property".
entries.ref: Regulations on unit money transactions and purchasing agents; BA16 Purchasing services.
entries.ask: The daughter of the case owner said that the amount I purchased on behalf of her was much more expensive than what she bought herself, and she suspected that I was taking kickbacks. Please help me compile a checklist format for explanation.

entries.t: Transporting a client in your own vehicle
entries.s: Most units prohibit the use of private vehicles to transport clients; in the event of an accident, the compulsory insurance will only cover basic insurance, and the optional insurance may not cover professional use, and you may bear civil and criminal liability.
entries.why: "Take him to the doctor by the way" is with good intentions, but an accident may cost you millions in compensation; long-term care has transportation and rehabilitation buses for this purpose.
steps: Check the unit's regulations first; do not upload unless explicitly allowed.

Transportation is needed: Assist in making appointments for long-term care transportation (BD03), rehabilitation buses, taxis (you can apply for charity taxi subsidies), or ask family members to take you.
If the unit allows it and it is insured: confirm that the vehicle insurance covers the purpose of carrying passengers, the client has accident insurance, and fill in the unit's outing application.
In principle, motorcycles should not be used to transport the elderly (the risk of falling is high and they cannot be fixed).
When an accident occurs, handle it as a "traffic accident on the way to service" and truthfully inform the company that the transport was by private car.
no: Don’t agree just because the family asks for it or the client is in a hurry.
Do not use motorcycles to transport clients.
Don't charge for gas or fares (turning it into a business activity, a violation of the Highway Code).
entries.rep: Supervision; Incident 110/119.
entries.ref: Articles 184 and 191-2 of the Civil Code (Liability of Drivers of Powered Vehicles); Compulsory Automobile Liability Insurance Law; Article 77 of the Highway Law (Operation of Motor Transport Industry Without Permit); Workplace Outings and Traffic Regulations.
entries.ask: The family asked me to drive the client to the follow-up consultation and I was willing to pay for the gas. Please help me sort out the reasons for refusal and alternative transportation resources.

entries.s: Only check the type of destination and travel in a manner regulated by the unit; the patient’s meals and fares are paid by the unit, and yours is stipulated by the unit; when the client is injured or property is lost when going out, responsibilities are clarified according to SOP and records.
entries.why: There is the most ambiguity when going out: Where is it reasonable to go? Who pays? Can the client treat me to a treat? Whose fault is it if he falls outside? If you make it clear first, nothing will happen.
steps: Scope: According to the approved contents of accompanied outings (shopping, walking, socializing, doing errands), special places (temple fairs, traveling, long distances) must be approved by the supervisor in advance.

Expenses: The client’s own consumption (meals, transportation fares, tickets) is paid by the client; your meal expenses and transportation fares are stipulated by the unit (mostly by the unit or not incurred). Treats by the client are not accepted. One drink or less will be handled and reported according to the unit’s regulations.
Time: limited to the approved hours. If time exceeds the limit, please report to the supervisor first.

Safety responsibility: Confirm the client's condition and weather before going out, and follow walking support and safety principles when going out; if the client is injured → handle, report, and record immediately, and the responsibility will be determined by the unit based on SOP and records.
The property of the case owner: Do not keep documents and large amounts of cash on your behalf; assist in finding, reporting to the police, and reporting if lost.
When the client goes out, he wants to see friends or engage in religious or political activities: he respects his autonomy but does not intervene or take a stand on his behalf.
no: Do not take the client to your home, your own store, or a friend’s store.
Do not accept payment for your meals or tickets.
Do not handle your own personal matters (getting money, buying groceries) when you are out.
entries.rep: Supervision; Injury or loss follows the abnormal event process.
entries.ref: Long-term care benefits and payment standards BA13 Accompanying outings; Regulations on company accompanying outings and accepting gifts; Articles 184 and 188 of the Civil Code.
entries.ask: The client insists on inviting me to lunch every time he goes out. If I don’t eat, he will get angry. Please give me a way to deal with it that can maintain the relationship and comply with the regulations.
